extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, librarians, and human-rights advocates interested in book censorship and library policy in Hong Kong
extracted.subtask_short: documenting book censorship in Hong Kong
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic compilation and timeline of incidents, policies, and lists of books censored, removed, or otherwise restricted in Hong Kong public, school, correctional and commercial settings, with references to international and professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: UNESCO Public Library Manifesto principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "collections and services should not be subject to any form of ideological, political or religious censorship, nor commercial pressures" (IFLA/UNESCO Public Library Manifesto quoted in article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative standard to judge library purchasing and de-selection; the manifesto frames that libraries exist to meet needs for lifelong learning, academic research and access to information and should 'adhere to the principle of safeguarding information freedom'. The page cites scholars who say current government actions violate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hong Kong Public Libraries selection policy (as stated)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Hong Kong Public Libraries selects and purchases library materials in accordance with the principles of the UNESCO Public Library Manifesto ... In the spirit of the Manifesto, the Hong Kong Public Libraries adheres to the principle of safeguarding information freedom when purchasing books and newspapers and will not censor publications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the official policy claim by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department/HKPL that is a benchmark for evaluating whether actual removals are consistent with stated library practice. The article contrasts the policy statement with subsequent removal actions as a measure of compliance or breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: UN Human Rights Committee recommendations (Article C, item 44)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UN Human Rights Committee in its concluding observations (Article C, item 44) states Hong Kong should: (a) Immediately stop censoring books and other material in public libraries, including school libraries, and reinstate the books and other material that have been removed for allegedly breaching the National Security Law or for being contrary to the interests of national security; (b) Publish a list of the books and materials that have been removed; (c) Take concrete steps necessary to ensure non-recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An authoritative international human-rights standard used to evaluate government practice. The three sub-items form clear actionable benchmarks: cessation of censorship and reinstatement, public disclosure of removed materials, and remedial measures to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFLA statements and Code of Ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the IFLA 'Statement on Libraries and Intellectual Freedom', 'Statement on Censorship', and 'IFLA Code of Ethics for Librarians and Other Information Workers' as normative documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IFLA documents are cited as international professional guidance supporting intellectual freedom and opposing censorship; they inform expectations for library conduct and professional responses to removal or restriction of materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hong Kong Library Association (HKLA) Code of Ethics / professional expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The article references the 'Code of Ethics – Hong Kong Library Association | HKLA' and criticizes that the Hong Kong Library Association and the Hong Kong Teacher-Librarians' Association 'have never expressed their concerns and taken corresponding actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local professional codes are presented as the standard librarians should follow (upholding information freedom, public access). The lack of professional response is used as an evaluative indicator of professional failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and professional responsibilities of librarians/teacher-librarians/education staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation that 'librarians, teacher-librarians, school quality assurance personnel (inspectors) of the Education Bureau, school management, teachers, etc. have [a duty] to uphold their professionalism and maintain the freedom of circulation and freedom of information' and that failure means loss of 'professional judgment, integrity and professionalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess actors' conduct: whether those working in libraries and schools are maintaining integrity and professional judgment when deciding on acquisitions, deaccessioning, censorship or self-censorship. The article treats professional norms as criteria for critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Security Law compliance as a de facto removal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the Law of the People's Republic of China on Safeguarding National Security in the Hong Kong SAR (effective July 1, 2020), media reports indicate libraries and other bodies have removed books and periodicals suspected of violating the law, some resulting in distributors and publishers being convicted and imprisoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This legal standard (or perceived legal risk) is described as the practical criterion driving removals and self-censorship. The article presents it as a cause of de-selection, a source of criminal risk for distributors/publishers, and a factor prompting institutional and individual caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctional Services Department (CSD) banned-books listing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Correctional Services Department has 'listed some books and periodicals as banned books' (i.e., prohibited for circulation to inmates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural criterion used by the CSD to decide which materials are allowed in prisons; the article treats it as an explicit institutional censorship policy and gives examples of titles and outcomes (refusal to accept certain donated books, judicial review proceedings).

rubrics_metrics.name: School-library self-censorship and redaction practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that some school principals and teachers responsible for national security education have been 'self-censoring' books in the school library — e.g., targeting books published in Taiwan and using stickers to block out 'Taiwan' and 'country', blackening out words with a black pen, or removing all books published in Taiwan from the shelves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an anti-pattern and operational behavior that departs from professional collection-management norms; useful as an evaluative criterion to identify overbroad or arbitrary restrictions and to assess whether schools are protecting or restricting students' access to information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital access suspension as a restriction criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where government schools suspended the e-book platform (HyRead) service and canceled online reading platforms to prevent access to content that might violate the National Security Law and the Basic Law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital-platform suspension is cited as a modality of censorship (not just physical deaccessioning). Evaluations should include whether blocking digital services is justified, proportionate, transparent, and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, documentation and completeness of banned-books listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Calls (and UN recommendations) for authorities to 'Publish a list of the books and materials that have been removed' and the article's own note: 'This is a dynamic list on books and periodicals that are known to have been censored and/or removed from shelves and/or reported in complaints. This may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency (public lists of removed items) and rigorous sourcing are treated as evaluation criteria for accountability. The page also emphasizes the need for reliable sourcing when compiling such lists and flags incompleteness as a limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book-fair participation/inclusivity and the organizer's transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that independent publishers were denied participation in the Hong Kong Book Fair without specific reasons, raising questions about the 'inclusivity and comprehensiveness of the book fair' and concerns regarding freedom of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate whether event organizers apply consistent, lawful, and transparent criteria for vendor participation and whether exclusion constitutes censorship or de facto suppression of certain viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with international human-rights instruments (UDHR/ICCPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that government actions 'seem to be in violation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and related conventions' and explicitly references the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights in relation to the UN Human Rights Committee observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International human-rights law (freedom of expression and information) is presented as a normative benchmark against which domestic removal and censorship practices should be measured.
